text.p: The mark was boosted in morning Europe from indications that the Bundesbank was unhappy with the EU stability pact which had unsettled the German currency.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing told the Financial Times he was not satisfied with the lack of "automaticity" in the accord, and said the debate over political policing of the pact was "not yet over".

"There are clear worries among Bundesbank officials that the European central bank and the stability pact are going to be more influenced by politics than they would like," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"In the very near term the tough talk by the Bundesbank could give the mark some temporary support," he added.

Germany's desire for automatic fines on states who overstep budget deficit limits after monetary union were tempered at the Dublin summit last week, with France winning its fight for political input into whether or not fines should be levied.
The mark firmed to 986.00/20 Italian lire by 0924 GMT from late Monday's European level of 984.42/77 and to 3.3756/58 French francs from 3.3743/47.
In its monthly report, the Bundesbank said the mark had now fully corrected its appreciation in 1995.
Exchange rate levels now broadly reflected economic fundamentals, the bank said.
The Bundesbank also said M3 monetary supply growth might overshoot its four to seven percent target at the end of 1996 but that German growth posed no threat to price stability.

Elsewhere, Sweden's Riksbank surprised few with a 25 basis-point cut in its key repo rate to 4.10 percent. The bank said the inflation outlook for the next two years was good, predicting inflation would total barely 1.5 percent in 1997 and around two percent in 1998.
The Swedish crown was unfazed, trading at 4.4050/80 per mark against Monday's European close of 4.3970/00.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet, together with members of the BOF's monetary policy council, holds a news conference on 1997 monetary policy at 1330 GMT.
Analysts expect Trichet to steer clear of controversy when he sets the central bank's policy targets, but believe he may hint at more official interest rate cuts.
